message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection (Thornbury District Council)

The pilot is a good basis for planning, and most of the arithmetic is correct. The cost table, the depreciation figure and the £74-per-tonne saving all check out.

Three of the study's central conclusions are contradicted by its own figures, however:

- **Participation in flats was not "broadly similar"** to houses. It was a third of the rate.
- **The tonnage projection uses a participation rate (64%) that appears nowhere in the pilot data.** The pilot figure is 57%.
- **The projected tonnage is almost double Brookfield's contracted capacity.** The service is therefore not fully local, and on corrected figures it is not fully funded.

## 1. Flats did not participate at a similar rate

| Housing type | Participation |
|---|---|
| Houses | 66% |
| Flats | **21%** |

Participation in flats was about a third of the rate in houses. This is the most important finding of the pilot, and the study reports the opposite: "broadly similar... without a separate approach for flats." The recommendation of a uniform service rests on that misreading.

Low participation in flats is common nationally. It usually reflects practical barriers, such as no space for an outdoor caddy, communal bin stores and long walks to set-out points, rather than resident attitudes. With about 10,400 flats in the district, a separate approach is needed. That typically means communal food bins at bin stores, with their own collection arrangements and costs.

## 2. The tonnage projection uses the wrong participation rate

Section 3 applies a 64% participation rate. The pilot's overall rate is 57%, and 64% doesn't correspond to any figure in Table 1.

Applying the pilot's own rates to the district's mix of 80% houses and 20% flats:

| | Households | Participation | Participating | kg per week | Tonnes per year |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 27,456 | 1.9 | 2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 2,184 | 1.4 | 159 |
| **Total** | **52,000** | **57%** | **29,640** | | **about 2,870** |

The corrected projection is **about 2,870 tonnes**, not 3,290. That reduces the disposal saving to about £212,500.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage

Brookfield has offered **up to 1,800 tonnes a year** until 2029. Even on the corrected figure of 2,870 tonnes, about **1,070 tonnes a year** has nowhere local to go. If a better approach for flats raises participation, the shortfall grows.

The study doesn't address this. The options all cost more than the study assumes:

- **The plant 46 miles away.** Food waste vehicles are small, so direct trips would take crews off their rounds for hours. A transfer or bulking arrangement would add costs.
- **Incineration of the excess.** This saves nothing and would likely not meet the requirement to treat separately collected food waste.

The claim that "treatment is local" holds for about 60% of the projected tonnage.

## 4. On corrected figures, the service is not fully funded

| | Annual figure |
|---|---|
| Cost, as stated | £733,400 |
| Saving on 1,800 t at Brookfield (× £74) | −£133,200 |
| Saving on remaining 1,070 t, at most (× £74, before haulage) | −£79,300 |
| **Net cost, best case** | **about £521,000** |
| Provisional new-burdens allocation | £520,000 |

Even in the best case, where the excess tonnage is treated at Brookfield's price with no extra haulage, the net cost slightly exceeds the allocation. Realistic haulage or transfer costs for the excess widen the gap. So do the missing cost lines below.

The original £30,000 headroom was in any case thin, under 5% of costs, against an allocation the study itself calls "provisional."

## 5. Cost lines that appear to be missing

The author describes the cost table as showing every line. Several items seem to be absent:

- **Vehicle cover.** Six vehicles for six rounds leaves no spare for breakdowns or servicing.
- **Crew cover.** There is no allowance for sickness and holiday cover, such as agency staff.
- **Staff on-costs.** If £34,000 is salary rather than total employment cost, employer National Insurance and pension contributions add about 25–30%.
- **Overheads.** Supervision, management, and the phone line and web support in Section 6 aren't costed.
- **Financing.** The £990,000 vehicle purchase needs funding up front, and only depreciation is shown, not interest.
- **Rounds.** There is no round modelling to show that six vehicles can reach all 52,000 households weekly. That is about 1,700 properties per vehicle per day over five days. It may be achievable, but it should be shown.

Also check whether the Council has already received government capital funding for vehicles and caddies. Many councils did, and if Thornbury has, the vehicle line may change.

## 6. Points to confirm

- **Incineration contract.** Confirm that removing food waste from the residual bin actually reduces the incineration bill. Some contracts include minimum-tonnage ("put or pay") terms.
- **Compostable liners.** Confirm that Brookfield accepts them. Some anaerobic digestion plants remove them as contamination, which affects both treatment and the liner budget.
- **Vehicle lead time.** Ordering in December for delivery in March is short. Check it with the supplier and allow for the Council's procurement process.
- **Statutory deadline.** My understanding is that the requirement for weekly food waste collections from households in England applied from 31 March 2026, with later dates only under transitional arrangements. Confirm the Council's position, as it affects how the April 2027 start should be presented to Cabinet.
- **Mobilisation.** Recruitment, training and caddy delivery to 52,000 households within February and March is tight, and a contingency plan would strengthen the timetable.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Survey figure.** The 81% satisfaction figure is from surveyed households. Respondents are likely to be the participating households, so it overstates satisfaction across all households.
- **Set-out rate.** Average weekly set-out understates participation, since some households take part but don't put a caddy out every week. Table 1 should say whether that is what "participation" means.

## Recommendation

Approving the roll-out is likely the right direction, since the service is required, but not on the current paper. Before Cabinet, the study should:

- **Correct the tonnage** to about 2,870 tonnes, using the pilot's own rates by housing type.
- **Design and cost a separate service for flats.**
- **Secure treatment capacity for the full tonnage.** Either negotiate more capacity at Brookfield or cost the alternatives.
- **Complete the cost table** with cover, on-costs, overheads and financing.
- **Present the funding position honestly.** On corrected figures, the service needs some Council contribution, unless the new-burdens allocation is confirmed at a higher level.
